title: Ἐπ’ ἀριστερά
titleEn: Idomeneus and Meriones Go Left — Iliad 13.266–360
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Meriones, who has come for a spear, answers Idomeneus: he has Trojan spoils of his own, but too far off to fetch, and he is no laggard in the fighting. Idomeneus replies that he knows his worth, and describes how an ambush shows the coward from the brave man; then he sends him to the hut to take a spear. The two go off to war like Ares and his son Terror, and Meriones asks where Idomeneus means to fight. Idomeneus says that the middle of the ships is held by the two Ajaxes and Teucer, that Hector will not burn the ships unless Zeus himself throws fire, and that Ajax would yield to Achilles only in running, and he turns to the left of the army. The Trojans see him blazing like flame and rush at him, and the fighting joins at the ships’ sterns in a glare of bronze. Meanwhile the two sons of Cronus work against each other: Zeus favours the Trojans to honour Achilles, and Poseidon, in secret and in a man’s likeness, rouses the Argives. Between them the gods draw tight over both armies a cord of strife that cannot be broken or loosed.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Μηριόνης πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ au Mērionēs pepnymenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Meriones spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Meriones spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: This is a reply formula: Meriones answers Idomeneus, who has just told him where to find spears (the previous part ends on that). The same line stands at 13.254. τόν ‘him’ is the old demonstrative that Homer uses where later Greek uses the article, and αὖ ‘in turn’ marks a new speaker. ηὔδα is the imperfect of αὐδάω ‘speak’, with the augment ηὐ-, and ἀντίον ‘face to face’ is an adverb. πεπνυμένος ‘prudent’ is a stock epithet of Meriones here, translated every time.

sentences.t:
καί τοι ἐμοὶ παρά τε κλισίῃ καὶ νηῒ μελαίνῃ
πόλλ’ ἔναρα Τρώων·
sentences.tr:
kai toi emoi para te klisiēi kai nēï melainēi
poll’ enara Trōōn·
sentences.l:
“And indeed to me also, beside my hut and my black ship,
many spoils of Trojans;
sentences.i: “I too have many spoils of the Trojans beside my hut and my black ship;
sentences.n: Meriones answers Idomeneus’ offer of spears in the last part: he has Trojan spoils of his own, though not at hand (next unit). καί … ἐμοί is ‘to me also’, ‘I too’. τοι is the particle ‘indeed’ (the same word as the pronoun ‘to you’, but not meant so here). The Greek has no verb: ‘to me (there are) many spoils’. ἔναρα are the arms stripped from a slain enemy. κλισίῃ is the dative of κλισίη ‘hut’, and νηῒ the dative of ναῦς ‘ship’, written with the diaeresis; μελαίνῃ ‘black’. The unit begins a speech.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ οὐ σχεδόν ἐστιν ἑλέσθαι.
sentences.tr: all’ ou schedon estin helesthai.
sentences.l: but not near is it to take them.
sentences.i: but they are not near enough to take.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ‘but’ turns from having spoils to not being able to reach them. οὐ σχεδόν ἐστιν ἑλέσθαι is ‘it is not near, to take (them)’: σχεδόν is the adverb ‘near’, and ἑλέσθαι the aorist middle infinitive of αἱρέω ‘take for oneself’. The spoils are too far off to fetch now, and that is why Meriones has come to Idomeneus’ hut. The unit begins in the middle of line 268.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ γὰρ οὐδ’ ἐμέ φημι λελασμένον ἔμμεναι ἀλκῆς,
ἀλλὰ μετὰ πρώτοισι μάχην ἀνὰ κυδιάνειραν
ἵσταμαι, ὁππότε νεῖκος ὀρώρηται πολέμοιο.
sentences.tr:
oude gar oud’ eme phēmi lelasmenon emmenai alkēs,
alla meta prōtoisi machēn ana kydianeiran
histamai, hoppote neikos orōrētai polemoio.
sentences.l:
For not even I, I say, am forgetful of might,
but among the first, through the man-glorifying battle,
I take my stand, whenever the quarrel of war has arisen.
sentences.i: For I say that not even I am forgetful of might, but through the battle that brings men glory I take my stand among the foremost, whenever the quarrel of war has arisen.
sentences.n: Meriones defends himself: lacking spoils to show, he says he is no shirker. οὐδὲ γὰρ οὐδ’ ἐμέ φημι is ‘for not even me, I say’: the negative belongs to the infinitive clause, ‘I say that not even I am …’, and not to φημι. λελασμένον is the perfect participle of λανθάνομαι ‘forget’, with the genitive ἀλκῆς ‘of might’, and ἔμμεναι is the epic infinitive ‘to be’ (= εἶναι). κυδιάνειραν ‘man-glorifying’ (κῦδος ‘glory’ + ἀνήρ ‘man’) is a stock epithet of battle, translated every time; ἀνά with the accusative is ‘through, throughout’. ὁππότε … ὀρώρηται is a perfect subjunctive middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, ‘has arisen’, in a general ‘whenever’ clause. νεῖκος is ‘quarrel’, the house word, and here means the fighting itself.

sentences.t:
ἄλλόν πού τινα μᾶλλον Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων
λήθω μαρνάμενος, σὲ δὲ ἴδμεναι αὐτὸν ὀΐω.
sentences.tr:
allon pou tina mallon Achaiōn chalkochitōnōn
lēthō marnamenos, se de idmenai auton oïō.
sentences.l:
Some other, perhaps, rather, of the bronze-shirted Achaeans
I escape the notice of, fighting; but you yourself, I think, know it.”
sentences.i: Perhaps it is some other of the bronze-shirted Achaeans, rather than you, who fails to notice me fighting; but you yourself, I think, know it.”
sentences.n: Meriones ends with a courteous sting: someone else may not see his deeds, but Idomeneus knows them. λήθω is ‘I escape the notice of’, and takes the accusative of the person who fails to notice (ἄλλον … τινα), with μαρνάμενος ‘fighting’ giving what goes unnoticed; πού ‘perhaps’ softens it and μᾶλλον ‘rather’ sets that other man against σέ ‘you’. ἴδμεναι is the epic infinitive of οἶδα ‘know’ (= εἰδέναι), with σὲ … αὐτόν as its subject after ὀΐω ‘I think’. χαλκοχιτώνων ‘bronze-shirted’ is the stock epithet of the Achaeans, translated every time. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ Ἰδομενεὺς Κρητῶν ἀγὸς ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aut’ Idomeneus Krētōn agos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To him in turn Idomeneus, leader of the Cretans, spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then Idomeneus, leader of the Cretans, spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: This is a reply formula: Idomeneus answers Meriones. The same line stands at 4.265 and again at 311 below. Κρητῶν ἀγός ‘leader of the Cretans’ is Idomeneus’ stock phrase (ἀγός from ἄγω ‘lead’), translated every time. τόν ‘him’ is the old demonstrative, αὖτε ‘in turn’, and ηὔδα the imperfect of αὐδάω ‘speak’, with the augment ηὐ-.

sentences.t: οἶδ’ ἀρετὴν οἷός ἐσσι·
sentences.tr: oid’ aretēn hoios essi·
sentences.l: “I know your excellence, of what sort you are;
sentences.i: “I know your excellence, what sort of man you are;
sentences.n: Idomeneus begins by saying that Meriones needs no proof of his courage. οἶδα is ‘I know’, and ἀρετήν ‘excellence’ is put first, as if the object of ‘know’, though the clause that follows (οἷός ἐσσι ‘of what sort you are’) says what is known; οἷος is the ‘of what sort’ word and ἐσσί the epic ‘you are’ (= εἶ). The unit begins a speech and ends in the middle of line 275.

sentences.t: τί σε χρὴ ταῦτα λέγεσθαι;
sentences.tr: ti se chrē tauta legesthai;
sentences.l: why must you talk these things over?
sentences.i: why must you talk of these things?
sentences.n: τί ‘why’ opens a rhetorical question. χρή ‘it is necessary’ takes σε as the subject of the infinitive: ‘why must you …’. λέγεσθαι is the middle infinitive of λέγω in its sense ‘talk over, recount’ (the same middle as λεγώμεθα at 292, ‘let us talk over’), and ταῦτα ‘these things’ are what Meriones has just said in his own defence. The unit begins in the middle of line 275.

sentences.t:
εἰ γὰρ νῦν παρὰ νηυσὶ λεγοίμεθα πάντες ἄριστοι
ἐς λόχον, ἔνθα μάλιστ’ ἀρετὴ διαείδεται ἀνδρῶν,
ἔνθ’ ὅ τε δειλὸς ἀνὴρ ὅς τ’ ἄλκιμος ἐξεφαάνθη·
sentences.tr:
ei gar nyn para nēusi legoimetha pantes aristoi
es lochon, entha malist’ aretē diaeidetai andrōn,
enth’ ho te deilos anēr hos t’ alkimos exephaanthē·
sentences.i: For if we were picked now beside the ships, all the best of us, for an ambush, where the excellence of men is most plainly seen, where the miserable man and the valiant man are shown for what they are:
sentences.n: Idomeneus builds an example: an ambush is the test that sorts the brave from the cowardly. The ‘if’ clause of 276 is a wish-form (εἰ γάρ + optative) used as a condition, and the result that answers it comes only at 287, after the description in between. λεγοίμεθα is the optative of the passive of λέγω in its older sense ‘pick out, choose’ (not ‘say’), and λόχος is an ambush, a party lying in wait. διαείδεται is a rare word, built on δια- and the root of ‘see’; ‘is made plain’ is the likeliest sense, not a certain one. ἐξεφαάνθη is an aorist passive of ἐκφαίνω ‘show forth’, a ‘gnomic’ aorist that states what always happens. δειλός is the house word ‘miserable’ and here means the man who turns out a coward; ἄλκιμος is ‘valiant’ (the noun ἀλκή ‘might’ stood at 269).

sentences.t:
τοῦ μὲν γάρ τε κακοῦ τρέπεται χρὼς ἄλλυδις ἄλλῃ,
οὐδέ οἱ ἀτρέμας ἧσθαι ἐρητύετ’ ἐν φρεσὶ θυμός,
ἀλλὰ μετοκλάζει καὶ ἐπ’ ἀμφοτέρους πόδας ἵζει,
sentences.tr:
tou men gar te kakou trepetai chrōs allydis allēi,
oude hoi atremas hēsthai erētyet’ en phresi thymos,
alla metoklazei kai ep’ amphoterous podas hizei,
sentences.l:
For of the base man the skin turns this way and that,
nor for him to sit motionless is held back the heart in his wits,
but he shifts about in a crouch and sits down on both feet,
sentences.i: For the skin of the base man turns this way and that, and his heart in his mind cannot be held to sit motionless, but he shifts about in a crouch and sits down on both feet,
sentences.n: Idomeneus now describes the coward, from the outside. τοῦ … κακοῦ is ‘of the base man’ (κακός of men in battle is ‘base’; its opposite ἀγαθός ‘good’ comes at 284), and the particles γάρ τε mark a general truth. τρέπεται χρὼς ἄλλυδις ἄλλῃ is literally ‘his skin turns this way and that’; the usual explanation is that his colour keeps changing, but the Greek says only ‘turns’. ἐρητύετ’ is the elided present middle of ἐρητύω ‘restrain’, so ‘his heart is not held (restrained) to sit still’; οἱ is ‘for him’, ἀτρέμας ‘motionless’, and ἧσθαι the infinitive of ἧμαι ‘sit’. μετοκλάζει is μετά ‘change’ + ὀκλάζω ‘crouch’: he keeps changing his crouch; ἐπ’ ἀμφοτέρους πόδας ἵζει ‘sits down on both feet’ is a squat. The exact posture is not clear; the picture is of a man who cannot keep still.

sentences.t:
ἐν δέ τέ οἱ κραδίη μεγάλα στέρνοισι πατάσσει
κῆρας ὀϊομένῳ, πάταγος δέ τε γίγνετ’ ὀδόντων·
sentences.tr:
en de te hoi kradiē megala sternoisi patassei
kēras oïomenōi, patagos de te gignet’ odontōn·
sentences.l:
and within him the heart greatly against his breast pounds
as he expects death-fates, and a chattering of teeth arises;
sentences.i: and within him the heart pounds hard against his breast as he expects the fates of death, and a chattering of teeth arises;
sentences.n: The coward’s body goes on being described, now from the inside. ἐν … πατάσσει is ‘pounds, strikes’ with ἐν as an adverb ‘within’, and οἱ ‘to him’ goes with the dative participle ὀϊομένῳ ‘expecting’ (ὀΐομαι ‘think, expect’). κῆρας are the κῆρες, the powers of death, in the plural: the house word is ‘death-fate’, ‘fates of death’, and it is kept apart from κῆρ ‘heart’. στέρνοισι ‘breast’ is στέρνον, kept apart from στῆθος ‘chest’. πάταγος ‘a clatter, chattering’ of ὀδόντων ‘teeth’; γίγνετ’ is the elided γίγνεται ‘arises, comes about’; τε again marks what is true in general.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ ἀγαθοῦ οὔτ’ ἂρ τρέπεται χρὼς οὔτέ τι λίην
ταρβεῖ, ἐπειδὰν πρῶτον ἐσίζηται λόχον ἀνδρῶν,
ἀρᾶται δὲ τάχιστα μιγήμεναι ἐν δαῒ λυγρῇ·
sentences.tr:
tou d’ agathou out’ ar trepetai chrōs oute ti liēn
tarbei, epeidan prōton esizētai lochon andrōn,
aratai de tachista migēmenai en daï lygrēi·
sentences.l:
But of the good man neither does the skin turn, nor very much
is he dismayed, when first he takes his seat in the ambush of men,
and he prays to be mingled, as quickly as possible, in the grievous fray:
sentences.i: But the good man’s skin does not change, nor is he very much dismayed, once he has first taken his seat in the ambush of men, and he prays to join the grievous fray as quickly as he can:
sentences.n: The brave man is the reverse of the coward just described. τοῦ δ’ ἀγαθοῦ ‘but of the good man’ answers τοῦ μὲν … κακοῦ (279). οὔτ’ ἂρ … οὔτέ τι λίην ‘neither … nor very much’: λίην is the Ionic λίαν ‘very much’, and ταρβεῖ is the contracted present of ταρβέω ‘be dismayed’. ἐπειδὰν πρῶτον ἐσίζηται is a subjunctive in a general clause, ‘whenever he first takes his seat in’, with λόχον ἀνδρῶν ‘an ambush of men’ (compare 277). ἀρᾶται ‘prays’ takes the infinitive μιγήμεναι, an aorist passive ‘to be mingled’, which means to join the fighting; δαΐ is the dative of δαΐς ‘fray, battle’, with λυγρῇ ‘grievous’.

sentences.t: οὐδέ κεν ἔνθα τεόν γε μένος καὶ χεῖρας ὄνοιτο.
sentences.tr: oude ken entha teon ge menos kai cheiras onoito.
sentences.l: Nor would one there make light of your might, at least, and your hands.
sentences.i: And no one there could make light of your might or your hands.
sentences.n: Here is the result that the ‘if’ of 276 was waiting for: in such a test, no one could fault Meriones. οὐδέ κεν … ὄνοιτο is ‘nor would … make light of’, κεν with the optative giving ‘would, could’; the subject is not named, ‘one’, ‘anyone’. ὄνοιτο is from ὄνομαι ‘make light of’, the house word (LSJ’s ‘find fault with’ is the gloss the tables turn down) and takes the accusatives μένος ‘might’ and χεῖρας ‘hands’. τεόν is the epic σόν ‘your’, ἔνθα ‘there’ (in the ambush), and γε ‘at least’.

sentences.t:
εἴ περ γάρ κε βλεῖο πονεύμενος ἠὲ τυπείης
οὐκ ἂν ἐν αὐχέν’ ὄπισθε πέσοι βέλος οὐδ’ ἐνὶ νώτῳ,
ἀλλά κεν ἢ στέρνων ἢ νηδύος ἀντιάσειε
πρόσσω ἱεμένοιο μετὰ προμάχων ὀαριστύν.
sentences.tr:
ei per gar ke bleio poneumenos ēe typeiēs
ouk an en auchen’ opisthe pesoi belos oud’ eni nōtōi,
alla ken ē sternōn ē nēdyos antiaseie
prossō hiemenoio meta promachōn oaristyn.
sentences.l:
For even if you were struck, toiling, or hit,
not on the neck behind would the shaft fall, nor in the back,
but it would meet either the breast or the belly
of you pressing forward to the close converse of the front-fighters.
sentences.i: For even if you were struck while toiling, or hit, the shaft would not fall on the back of your neck or in your back, but would meet your breast or your belly as you pressed forward to the close exchange among the foremost fighters.
sentences.n: Idomeneus adds a second proof: even a wound would be taken from the front. εἴ περ γάρ κε βλεῖο … ἠὲ τυπείης is ‘for even if you were struck … or hit’; βλεῖο (an aorist optative, middle in form and passive in sense) and τυπείης (an aorist optative passive) are 2nd person singular, of βάλλω and τύπτω, and πονεύμενος is ‘toiling’, at one’s work in the fight. οὐκ ἂν … πέσοι βέλος is ‘a shaft would not fall’, ἐν αὐχέν’ ὄπισθε ‘on the neck from behind’, οὐδ’ ἐνὶ νώτῳ ‘nor in the back’. ἀλλά κεν ἢ στέρνων ἢ νηδύος ἀντιάσειε is ‘but it would meet either breast or belly’, ἀντιάω taking the genitive, with the same subject βέλος. πρόσσω ἱεμένοιο is a genitive ‘of you pressing forward’ (ἵεμαι ‘press on’), and μετά with the accusative is ‘to join, in quest of’. ὀαριστύς is literally ‘close talk, intimate conversation’; here it is a figure for fighting at close quarters, among the προμάχοι ‘front-fighters’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε μηκέτι ταῦτα λεγώμεθα νηπύτιοι ὣς
ἑσταότες, μή πού τις ὑπερφιάλως νεμεσήσῃ·
sentences.tr:
all’ age mēketi tauta legōmetha nēpytioi hōs
hestaotes, mē pou tis hyperphialōs nemesēsēi·
sentences.l:
But come, let us no longer talk these things over, like babes,
standing, lest someone beyond measure feel resentment;
sentences.i: But come, let us no longer stand here talking these things over like children, in case someone should resent it beyond measure;
sentences.n: Idomeneus cuts the talk short. ἀλλ’ ἄγε is ‘but come’, and μηκέτι … λεγώμεθα a hortatory subjunctive, middle: ‘let us no longer talk over (to one another)’; νηπύτιοι ὣς is ‘like children’, and ἑσταότες the perfect participle of ἵστημι ‘standing’. μή πού τις … νεμεσήσῃ is ‘lest anyone perhaps feel resentment’, μή with the subjunctive, νεμεσάω being the verb of righteous indignation that the house text renders ‘resentment’; ὑπερφιάλως ‘beyond measure’ is the adverb of ὑπερφίαλος ‘overweening’ (the house word for the adverb; ‘overbearing’ belongs to ὑπερηνορέων).

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ σύ γε κλισίην δὲ κιὼν ἕλευ ὄβριμον ἔγχος.
sentences.tr: alla sy ge klisiēn de kiōn heleu obrimon enchos.
sentences.l: But you, at least, to the hut going, take a mighty spear.”
sentences.i: But you, at least, go to the hut and take a mighty spear.”
sentences.n: Idomeneus sends Meriones for the spear he came for. κλισίην δέ is κλισίην with the suffix -δε ‘to’, ‘to the hut’; this is the hut in which, he said at 260–261, the spears stand. σύ γε ‘you at least’, κιών the participle of κίω ‘go’, and ἕλευ the aorist middle imperative of αἱρέω ‘take for yourself’. ὄβριμον ἔγχος is ‘a mighty spear’ (ὄβριμος ‘mighty’). The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, Μηριόνης δὲ θοῷ ἀτάλαντος Ἄρηϊ
καρπαλίμως κλισίηθεν ἀνείλετο χάλκεον ἔγχος,
βῆ δὲ μετ’ Ἰδομενῆα μέγα πτολέμοιο μεμηλώς.
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, Mērionēs de thoōi atalantos Arēï
karpalimōs klisiēthen aneileto chalkeon enchos,
bē de met’ Idomenēa mega ptolemoio memēlōs.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and Meriones, the equal of swift Ares,
swiftly from the hut took up a bronze spear,
and went after Idomeneus, greatly concerned with war.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Meriones, the equal of swift Ares, swiftly took a bronze spear from the hut and went after Idomeneus, greatly concerned with war.
sentences.n: Meriones does as he is told. ὣς φάτο ‘so he spoke’ closes the speech. θοῷ ἀτάλαντος Ἄρηϊ ‘the equal of swift Ares’ (ἀτάλαντος ‘of equal weight’) is Meriones’ stock epithet, translated every time; the same words open 328. κλισίηθεν is ‘from the hut’ (suffix -θεν), ἀνείλετο the aorist middle of ἀναιρέω ‘took up for himself’, and χάλκεον ἔγχος ‘a bronze spear’. βῆ is the unaugmented aorist ‘he went’, and μετ’ Ἰδομενῆα ‘after Idomeneus’. μέγα πτολέμοιο μεμηλώς is ‘greatly concerned with war’: μεμηλώς is the perfect participle of μέλω (with the genitive; the house phrase, as in μέγα πλούτοιο μεμηλώς ‘greatly concerned with wealth’, 5.708), and πτολέμοιο is the epic form of πολέμοιο.

sentences.t:
οἷος δὲ βροτολοιγὸς Ἄρης πόλεμον δὲ μέτεισι,
τῷ δὲ Φόβος φίλος υἱὸς ἅμα κρατερὸς καὶ ἀταρβὴς
ἕσπετο, ὅς τ’ ἐφόβησε ταλάφρονά περ πολεμιστήν·
sentences.tr:
hoios de brotoloigos Arēs polemon de meteisi,
tōi de Phobos philos huios hama krateros kai atarbēs
hespeto, hos t’ ephobēse talaphrona per polemistēn·
sentences.l:
And as mortal-ruining Ares goes to war,
and with him Terror, his dear son, strong and unafraid,
follows, who puts to flight even an enduring-minded warrior:
sentences.i: As when Ares, the ruin of mortals, goes to war, and with him follows Terror, his dear son, strong and unafraid, who puts to flight even a steadfast warrior:
sentences.n: The poet compares Idomeneus and Meriones, setting out together, to Ares and his son; the likeness is made explicit at 304. οἷος … μέτεισι is ‘such as Ares when he goes’ (μέτειμι ‘go after, go among’; πόλεμον δέ ‘to war’, with the suffix -δε), and τῷ δέ ‘and with him’ begins the second half. βροτολοιγός ‘ruin of mortals’ (βροτός + λοιγός) is Ares’ stock epithet, translated every time. Φόβος is the power Terror, Ares’ dear son; ἀταρβής is ‘unafraid’; ἕσπετο is the aorist of ἕπομαι ‘follow’ (here in a general statement, so ‘follows’). ὅς τ’ ἐφόβησε is a general statement in the aorist: ‘who (always) puts to flight’. ταλάφρονα is built on τλάω ‘endure’ and φρήν ‘mind’ and is close to ταλασίφρων, so it takes the same English; περ ‘even’; πολεμιστής ‘warrior’.

sentences.t:
τὼ μὲν ἄρ’ ἐκ Θρῄκης Ἐφύρους μέτα θωρήσσεσθον,
ἠὲ μετὰ Φλεγύας μεγαλήτορας·
sentences.tr:
tō men ar’ ek Thrēikēs Ephyrous meta thōrēssesthon,
ēe meta Phlegyas megalētoras·
sentences.l:
The two then from Thrace toward the Ephyri arm themselves,
or toward the great-spirited Phlegyes;
sentences.i: Those two arm themselves for the Ephyri, out of Thrace, or for the great-spirited Phlegyes;
sentences.n: Ares and Terror, the pair of the comparison, are pictured setting out from Thrace, to attack one of two peoples. τὼ μέν is the dual ‘those two’ and θωρήσσεσθον the dual ‘they arm themselves’; μέτα (accented because it follows its noun) and μετά with the accusative mean ‘after, toward’. Ἐφύρους are the Ephyri, and Φλεγύας the Phlegyes; the lines do not say where either people lived. μεγαλήτορας ‘great-spirited’ is a stock epithet, translated every time. The unit ends in the middle of line 302.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρα τώ γε
ἔκλυον ἀμφοτέρων, ἑτέροισι δὲ κῦδος ἔδωκαν·
sentences.tr:
oud’ ara tō ge
eklyon amphoterōn, heteroisi de kydos edōkan·
sentences.l:
and not, then, those two
listened to both, but to others gave glory:
sentences.i: and they do not listen to both, but give glory to others;
sentences.n: The point of the comparison: Ares and Terror do not do what either people prays for. οὐδ’ ἄρα τώ γε is ‘and the two of them did not’, τώ being the dual; ἔκλυον ‘listened to’ takes the genitive ἀμφοτέρων ‘both’ (the Ephyri and the Phlegyes). ἑτέροισι is the dative plural of ἕτερος, ‘to others’; κῦδος is ‘glory’. The Greek leaves open who the ‘others’ are, and whether ‘not … both’ means ‘neither’. ἔκλυον and ἔδωκαν are aorists in a general statement about what the pair do, so the English translation uses the present. The unit begins in the middle of line 302.

sentences.t:
τοῖοι Μηριόνης τε καὶ Ἰδομενεὺς ἀγοὶ ἀνδρῶν
ἤϊσαν ἐς πόλεμον κεκορυθμένοι αἴθοπι χαλκῷ.
sentences.tr:
toioi Mērionēs te kai Idomeneus agoi andrōn
ēïsan es polemon kekorythmenoi aithopi chalkōi.
sentences.l:
Such were Meriones and Idomeneus, leaders of men,
as they went to war, armed with the fire-faced bronze.
sentences.i: Such were Meriones and Idomeneus, leaders of men, as they went to war, armed with bronze that has the look of fire.
sentences.n: The comparison is closed: the two Cretans are the Ares and Terror just described. τοῖοι ‘such’ is the epic form of τοιοῦτοι, ἀγοὶ ἀνδρῶν ‘leaders of men’ (ἀγός ‘leader’), and ἤϊσαν the imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’. κεκορυθμένοι is the perfect passive participle of κορύσσω ‘arm, equip with a helmet’, and αἴθοπι χαλκῷ ‘fire-faced bronze’, i.e. bronze that has the look of fire (αἴθω ‘burn’ + ὤψ ‘face, look’), is a house phrase.

sentences.t: τὸν καὶ Μηριόνης πρότερος πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπε·
sentences.tr: ton kai Mērionēs proteros pros mython eeipe·
sentences.l: Him also Meriones, first, with a word addressed:
sentences.i: Meriones spoke to him first, with these words:
sentences.n: A speech-introduction: Meriones asks the question that the rest of the passage answers. This is the Odyssey’s formula for the first speaker (τὸν καὶ … πρότερος πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπε, as at Odyssey 16.460 and 17.74), and it takes the Odyssey’s English. πρὸς … ἔειπε is a tmesis, the preverb separated from the verb, for προσεῖπε ‘addressed’. καί is part of the formula (‘him also’); πρότερος ‘first’.

sentences.t: Δευκαλίδη πῇ τὰρ μέμονας καταδῦναι ὅμιλον;
sentences.tr: Deukalidē pēi tar memonas katadynai homilon;
sentences.l: “Deucalion’s-son, where then do you intend to go down into the throng?
sentences.i: “Son of Deucalion, where, then, do you intend to go down into the throng?
sentences.n: Meriones asks Idomeneus where he means to fight. Δευκαλίδη is the vocative of the patronymic, ‘son of Deucalion’; Idomeneus’ father is Deucalion. πῇ τὰρ is ‘where, then’: τὰρ is a particle compound that adds ‘then’ to the question. μέμονας is a perfect with present sense, ‘you are minded, you intend’, and καταδῦναι the aorist infinitive of καταδύω ‘go down into’, with ὅμιλον ‘throng’ as its goal. The unit begins a speech.

sentences.t:
ἢ ἐπὶ δεξιόφιν παντὸς στρατοῦ, ἦ ἀνὰ μέσσους,
ἦ ἐπ’ ἀριστερόφιν;
sentences.tr:
ē epi dexiophin pantos stratou, ē ana messous,
ē ep’ aristerophin;
sentences.l:
Either to the right of the whole army, or through the middle,
or to the left?
sentences.i: To the right of the whole army, or through the middle, or to the left?
sentences.n: Meriones lists the three places Idomeneus might go. δεξιόφιν and ἀριστερόφιν have the old suffix -φιν, here ‘on the right’, ‘on the left’, with ἐπί ‘to’; παντὸς στρατοῦ is ‘of the whole army’. ἀνὰ μέσσους is ‘through the middle’ (μέσσους the epic double-σ accusative plural of μέσος, ‘through the midst of them’). The three ἢ … ἦ … ἦ are ‘either … or … or’. The unit ends in the middle of line 309.

sentences.t:
ἐπεὶ οὔ ποθι ἔλπομαι οὕτω
δεύεσθαι πολέμοιο κάρη κομόωντας Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.tr:
epei ou pothi elpomai houtō
deuesthai polemoio karē komoōntas Achaious.
sentences.l:
since not anywhere do I expect so to be in want of war
the long-haired-of-head Achaeans.”
sentences.i: For I do not expect the long-haired Achaeans to be so short of war anywhere.”
sentences.n: Meriones gives his reason for asking: ἐπεί ‘since’. οὔ ποθι ἔλπομαι is ‘I do not expect anywhere’ (ἔλπομαι ‘expect’, which in Homer need not be hopeful). δεύεσθαι with the genitive means ‘to lack, to be short of’, so ‘to be short of war’, an odd phrase: the Greek says only that the Achaeans are nowhere ‘wanting in war’, and does not settle whether Meriones means that fighting is hot all along the line or that no part of the line lacks fighters. κάρη κομόωντας Ἀχαιούς ‘the long-haired(-of-head) Achaeans’ is a stock epithet, translated every time. The unit begins in the middle of line 309 and ends the speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ Ἰδομενεὺς Κρητῶν ἀγὸς ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aut’ Idomeneus Krētōn agos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To him in turn Idomeneus, leader of the Cretans, spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then Idomeneus, leader of the Cretans, spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: This is the reply formula again: Idomeneus answers Meriones’ question. The line is the same as 274 and as 4.265. Κρητῶν ἀγός ‘leader of the Cretans’ is his stock phrase, translated every time.

sentences.t:
νηυσὶ μὲν ἐν μέσσῃσιν ἀμύνειν εἰσὶ καὶ ἄλλοι
Αἴαντές τε δύω Τεῦκρός θ’, ὃς ἄριστος Ἀχαιῶν
τοξοσύνῃ, ἀγαθὸς δὲ καὶ ἐν σταδίῃ ὑσμίνῃ·
sentences.tr:
nēusi men en messēisin amynein eisi kai alloi
Aiantes te dyō Teukros th’, hos aristos Achaiōn
toxosynēi, agathos de kai en stadiēi hysminēi·
sentences.i: “Among the ships in the middle there are others as well to defend them, the two Ajaxes and Teucer, who is the best of the Achaeans at archery, and good also in the battle where men stand their ground;
sentences.n: Idomeneus answers the question region by region, beginning with the centre, which is already held. νηυσὶ μὲν ἐν μέσσῃσιν is ‘among the ships in the middle’ (μέσσῃσιν the epic dative plural, agreeing with νηυσί), and the μέν waits for the contrast at 326. ἀμύνειν εἰσί is ‘there are (men) to defend’, an infinitive of purpose; καὶ ἄλλοι ‘others as well’. Αἴαντες δύω are the two Ajaxes (the son of Telamon and the son of Oileus), and Τεῦκρος is the archer Teucer. τοξοσύνῃ ‘in archery’ is a dative of respect. ἀγαθός is ‘good’, and ἐν σταδίῃ ὑσμίνῃ ‘in the standing battle’ is fighting hand to hand and on foot, holding one’s ground (σταδίη from ἵστημι ‘stand’). The unit begins a speech.

sentences.t:
οἵ μιν ἅδην ἐλόωσι καὶ ἐσσύμενον πολέμοιο
Ἕκτορα Πριαμίδην, καὶ εἰ μάλα καρτερός ἐστιν.
sentences.tr:
hoi min hadēn eloōsi kai essymenon polemoio
Hektora Priamidēn, kai ei mala karteros estin.
sentences.l:
who him to the full will drive, though rushing on of war,
Hector, Priam’s-son, even if he is very strong.
sentences.i: They will drive him to his fill of war, eager as he is for it, Hector, son of Priam, even if he is very strong.
sentences.n: The three defenders will deal with Hector. οἵ ‘who’ picks up Αἴαντες and Τεῦκρος; μιν is Hector, named at the start of line 316. ἐλόωσι is an epic uncontracted form of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’ with a future sense, ‘they will drive’, and ἅδην means ‘to the full, to satiety’ with the genitive: πολέμοιο ‘of war’ can go with ἅδην (‘his fill of war’) or with ἐσσύμενον (‘rushing toward war’); the sense is the same either way, that they will give him his fill of fighting. ἐσσύμενον is the perfect participle of σεύομαι ‘rush, be eager’, with καί ‘even’; Πριαμίδην is the patronymic ‘son of Priam’; καρτερός ‘strong’.

sentences.t:
αἰπύ οἱ ἐσσεῖται μάλα περ μεμαῶτι μάχεσθαι
κείνων νικήσαντι μένος καὶ χεῖρας ἀάπτους
νῆας ἐνιπρῆσαι, ὅτε μὴ αὐτός γε Κρονίων
ἐμβάλοι αἰθόμενον δαλὸν νήεσσι θοῇσιν.
sentences.tr:
aipy hoi esseitai mala per memaōti machesthai
keinōn nikēsanti menos kai cheiras aaptous
nēas eniprēsai, hote mē autos ge Kroniōn
embaloi aithomenon dalon nēessi thoēisin.
sentences.l:
Steep will it be for him, though very eager to fight,
having conquered the might and untouchable hands of those men,
to set the ships on fire, unless the son of Cronus himself
should throw a burning brand upon the swift ships.
sentences.i: It will be steep for him, eager though he is to fight, once he has overcome the might and the irresistible hands of those men, to set the ships on fire, unless the son of Cronus himself should hurl a burning brand upon the swift ships.
sentences.n: Idomeneus’ conclusion about Hector: he cannot burn the ships by his own strength; only Zeus can give him fire. αἰπύ is neuter, ‘steep’, said of a hard task (as in αἰπὺς ὄλεθρος), so αἰπύ οἱ ἐσσεῖται is ‘it will be steep for him’. μάλα περ μεμαῶτι μάχεσθαι is ‘though very eager to fight’, a dative participle agreeing with οἱ; so is νικήσαντι, ‘having overcome’, whose objects are μένος ‘might’ and χεῖρας ἀάπτους ‘untouchable, irresistible hands’ (ἀάπτους is of unknown sense; the house words are ‘untouchable’ in the first English and ‘irresistible’ in the second, both traditional guesses), and κείνων is the epic form of ἐκείνων ‘of those men’. The infinitive νῆας ἐνιπρῆσαι ‘to set the ships on fire’ completes αἰπύ. ὅτε μή is ‘unless’, with the optative ἐμβάλοι ‘should throw in’; Κρονίων is Zeus, δαλός a firebrand, αἰθόμενον ‘burning’, and νήεσσι θοῇσιν the epic dative plural ‘upon the swift ships’.

sentences.t:
ἀνδρὶ δέ κ’ οὐκ εἴξειε μέγας Τελαμώνιος Αἴας,
ὃς θνητός τ’ εἴη καὶ ἔδοι Δημήτερος ἀκτὴν
χαλκῷ τε ῥηκτὸς μεγάλοισί τε χερμαδίοισιν.
sentences.tr:
andri de k’ ouk eixeie megas Telamōnios Aias,
hos thnētos t’ eiē kai edoi Dēmēteros aktēn
chalkōi te rhēktos megaloisi te chermadioisin.
sentences.l:
And to a man would not yield great Telamonian Ajax,
who is mortal and eats the meal of Demeter,
breakable by bronze and by great stones.
sentences.i: Great Telamonian Ajax would not give way to any man who is mortal and eats the meal of Demeter and can be broken by bronze and by great stones.
sentences.n: Idomeneus now speaks of the great Ajax, who is the other firm defender of the ships. κε with the optative in ἀνδρὶ δέ κ’ οὐκ εἴξειε is ‘would not’, and εἴκω takes the dative: ‘give way to a man’. The relative clause that follows (ὃς … εἴη καὶ ἔδοι, both optatives) says which sort of man: a mortal, who ‘eats the meal of Demeter’, that is, lives on bread as men do (this ἀκτή is ground grain, a different word from the ἀκτή that means ‘shore’), and who is ῥηκτός ‘breakable’ (a verbal adjective of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’) by χαλκῷ ‘bronze’ and by μεγάλοισι χερμαδίοισιν ‘great stones’. Τελαμώνιος tells this Ajax from the other.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἂν Ἀχιλλῆϊ ῥηξήνορι χωρήσειεν
ἔν γ’ αὐτοσταδίῃ·
sentences.tr:
oud’ an Achillēï rhēxēnori chōrēseien
en g’ autostadiēi·
sentences.l:
Nor to Achilles, man-breaking, would he give way
in close standing-fight, at least;
sentences.i: Nor would he give way to Achilles, the man-breaker, at least in close combat;
sentences.n: Even Achilles, Idomeneus says, would not make Ajax give ground in a fight at close quarters. οὐδ’ ἂν … χωρήσειεν is ‘nor would he give way’ (χωρέω ‘go off, give ground’, with the dative), carrying on the ‘would not yield’ of 321. ῥηξήνορι is the dative of ῥηξήνωρ, ‘man-breaker’ (ῥήγνυμι ‘break’ + ἀνήρ), Achilles’ stock epithet, translated every time; it is not known whether men or their ranks are broken. αὐτοσταδίῃ is a rare noun, ‘a fight at close quarters, standing on the spot’ (αὐτός + σταδίη, compare 314); ἔν … γε ‘in … at least’. Ἀχιλλῆϊ is spelled with double λ here, and Ἀχιλῆα with one at 348. The unit ends in the middle of line 325.

sentences.t: ποσὶ δ’ οὔ πως ἔστιν ἐρίζειν.
sentences.tr: posi d’ ou pōs estin erizein.
sentences.l: but with feet it is in no way possible to rival.
sentences.i: but in speed of foot there is no way to rival him.
sentences.n: The contrast to the last unit: in a fight Ajax would not yield, but in running no one competes with Achilles. ποσί is the dative ‘with the feet’, the thing in which the contest would be; οὔ πως ἔστιν ‘there is in no way’ (it is not possible), ἐρίζειν ‘to rival’, with the dative understood (‘with him’). The unit begins in the middle of line 325.

sentences.t:
νῶϊν δ’ ὧδ’ ἐπ’ ἀριστέρ’ ἔχε στρατοῦ, ὄφρα τάχιστα
εἴδομεν ἠέ τῳ εὖχος ὀρέξομεν, ἦέ τις ἡμῖν.
sentences.tr:
nōïn d’ hōd’ ep’ arister’ eche stratou, ophra tachista
eidomen ēe tōi euchos orexomen, ēe tis hēmin.
sentences.l:
But for us two thus to the left of the army hold on, so that quickest
we may know whether to someone we shall grant a boast, or someone to us.”
sentences.i: As for us two, keep on this way, to the left of the army, so that we may find out as quickly as possible whether we shall grant the triumph to someone, or someone to us.”
sentences.n: Idomeneus ends by telling Meriones where they will go: to the left. νῶϊν is the dual dative ‘for us two’. ὧδ’ ἐπ’ ἀριστέρ’ ἔχε στρατοῦ is ‘thus to the left of the army hold’: ἔχε is the imperative of ἔχω ‘hold’, used here without an object for ‘keep on (your course)’, and the next unit shows Meriones taking the lead; ἀριστέρ’ is the elided neuter plural, used as an adverb ‘on the left’. ὄφρα … εἴδομεν is a purpose clause with the short-vowel subjunctive of οἶδα ‘know’. τῳ is the indefinite ‘to someone’, and ὀρέξομεν the subjunctive of ὀρέγω ‘hold out, grant’; εὖχος is the ‘boast’, that of which one may be proud, a triumph. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, Μηριόνης δὲ θοῷ ἀτάλαντος Ἄρηϊ
ἦρχ’ ἴμεν, ὄφρ’ ἀφίκοντο κατὰ στρατὸν ᾗ μιν ἀνώγει,
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, Mērionēs de thoōi atalantos Arēï
ērch’ imen, ophr’ aphikonto kata straton hēi min anōgei,
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and Meriones, the equal of swift Ares,
led the way to go, until they came through the army where he bade him,
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Meriones, the equal of swift Ares, led the way, until they came through the army to where he had bidden him,
sentences.n: The action resumes: Meriones leads, and the two reach the left. ὣς φάτο closes Idomeneus’ speech; the first line is the same as 295. ἦρχ’ ἴμεν is the imperfect of ἄρχω ‘lead’ with the epic infinitive ἴμεν (= ἰέναι) ‘to go’: ‘led the way going’. ὄφρ’ ἀφίκοντο is ‘until they arrived’ (ἀφικνέομαι), κατὰ στρατόν ‘through the army’, and ᾗ the relative adverb ‘where’. μιν is Meriones and the unnamed subject of ἀνώγει ‘bade’ is Idomeneus. The edition ends the paragraph at this comma, and the sentence goes on in the next unit with a change of subject.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὡς Ἰδομενῆα ἴδον φλογὶ εἴκελον ἀλκὴν
αὐτὸν καὶ θεράποντα σὺν ἔντεσι δαιδαλέοισι,
κεκλόμενοι καθ’ ὅμιλον ἐπ’ αὐτῷ πάντες ἔβησαν·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ hōs Idomenēa idon phlogi eikelon alkēn
auton kai theraponta syn entesi daidaleoisi,
keklomenoi kath’ homilon ep’ autōi pantes ebēsan·
sentences.i: And when they saw Idomeneus, like a flame in might, himself and his attendant, with their finely wrought gear, they called out and all went at him through the throng;
sentences.n: The Trojans on that wing notice the pair. οἳ δ’ ‘and they’ is the Trojans, not yet named in the sentence. ὡς … ἴδον is ‘when they saw’ (unaugmented aorist of εἶδον), and φλογὶ εἴκελον ἀλκήν is ‘like flame in might’: φλογί is the dative of likeness and ἀλκήν an accusative of respect. αὐτὸν καὶ θεράποντα is ‘himself and his attendant’, that is Meriones; σὺν ἔντεσι δαιδαλέοισι ‘with finely wrought gear’ (ἔντεα ‘gear, arms’, with the epic dative ending -οισι). The last line is the same as 11.460, where the Trojans close on the wounded Odysseus: κεκλόμενοι ‘calling out’, καθ’ ὅμιλον ‘through the throng’, ἐπ’ αὐτῷ … ἔβησαν ‘went at him’.

sentences.t: τῶν δ’ ὁμὸν ἵστατο νεῖκος ἐπὶ πρυμνῇσι νέεσσιν.
sentences.tr: tōn d’ homon histato neikos epi prymnēisi neessin.
sentences.l: and of them a common quarrel stood at the sterns of the ships.
sentences.i: And a quarrel common to both sides arose at the sterns of the ships.
sentences.n: The fighting is now joined at the ships. τῶν is ‘of them’, both sides; ὁμὸν νεῖκος is ‘a common quarrel’ (νεῖκος ‘quarrel’ is the house word; here it is the fighting itself), one that both sides share, in the same place (compare ὁμόσ’ at 337). ἵστατο is the imperfect middle of ἵστημι, ‘stood, was set up’. ἐπὶ πρυμνῇσι νέεσσιν is ‘at the sterns of the ships’: πρυμνῇσι is the adjective from πρύμνη ‘stern’, and νέεσσιν the epic dative plural of ναῦς.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅθ’ ὑπὸ λιγέων ἀνέμων σπέρχωσιν ἄελλαι
ἤματι τῷ ὅτε τε πλείστη κόνις ἀμφὶ κελεύθους,
οἵ τ’ ἄμυδις κονίης μεγάλην ἱστᾶσιν ὀμίχλην,
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hoth’ hypo ligeōn anemōn sperchōsin aellai
ēmati tōi hote te pleistē konis amphi keleuthous,
hoi t’ amydis koniēs megalēn histasin omichlēn,
sentences.l:
And as when under clear winds the blasts rush on,
on the day when there is most dust about the ways,
and these together raise a great mist of dust,
sentences.i: And as when the storms rush on, driven by clear-sounding winds, on the day when dust lies thickest about the ways, and the winds together raise a great mist of dust,
sentences.n: A simile for the clash: the sentence begins ὡς δ’ ὅθ’ ‘and as when’ and is completed by ὣς ἄρα ‘so’ at 337. ὑπὸ λιγέων ἀνέμων is ‘under clear(-sounding) winds’, the winds driving them; ἄελλαι ‘blasts, storms’ is the subject of σπέρχωσιν, the subjunctive of σπέρχω ‘press on, rush’. ἤματι τῷ ὅτε τε is ‘on the day when’, and πλείστη κόνις ‘the most dust’ (superlative of πολύς), ἀμφὶ κελεύθους ‘about the ways’ (κέλευθος ‘way’, here the roads). οἵ is masculine plural, so it picks up the winds, not the feminine ἄελλαι: they together (ἄμυδις) set up (ἱστᾶσιν) a great ὀμίχλη ‘mist’ of dust (κονίης is a genitive of material).

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα τῶν ὁμόσ’ ἦλθε μάχη, μέμασαν δ’ ἐνὶ θυμῷ
ἀλλήλους καθ’ ὅμιλον ἐναιρέμεν ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ.
sentences.tr:
hōs ara tōn homos’ ēlthe machē, memasan d’ eni thymōi
allēlous kath’ homilon enairemen oxeï chalkōi.
sentences.l:
so then of these to the same place came the fight, and they were eager in heart
one another through the throng to slay with sharp bronze.
sentences.i: so the fighting of these men came together in one place, and they were eager in their hearts to slay one another through the throng with sharp bronze.
sentences.n: The simile’s second half. ὣς ἄρα answers ὡς δ’ ὅθ’ (334). ὁμόσε is ‘to the same place’; τῶν ‘of these’; μάχη ‘fight’. μέμασαν is a perfect of μάω with present force, ‘they were eager’, and ἐναιρέμεν the epic infinitive of ἐναίρω ‘slay’. ἀλλήλους ‘one another’, καθ’ ὅμιλον ‘through the throng’, ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ ‘with sharp bronze’.

sentences.t:
ἔφριξεν δὲ μάχη φθισίμβροτος ἐγχείῃσι
μακρῇς, ἃς εἶχον ταμεσίχροας·
sentences.tr:
ephrixen de machē phthisimbrotos encheiēisi
makrēis, has eichon tamesichroas·
sentences.l:
And bristled the mortal-destroying battle with spears,
long, which they held, skin-cutting;
sentences.i: And the mortal-destroying battle bristled with long spears, which they held, spears that cut the skin;
sentences.n: The battle is pictured as a bristling line of spears. ἔφριξεν is the aorist of φρίσσω ‘bristle’, and the subject is μάχη, with φθισίμβροτος ‘mortal-destroying’ (φθίω ‘waste, destroy’ + βροτός ‘mortal’) as its stock epithet, translated every time. ἐγχείῃσι μακρῇς ‘with long spears’ is a dative of means with the epic ending -ῃσι. ἃς εἶχον ταμεσίχροας is ‘which they held, skin-cutting’ (τάμνω ‘cut’ + χρώς ‘skin’); ταμεσίχροας agrees with ἃς. The unit ends in the middle of line 340.

sentences.t:
ὄσσε δ’ ἄμερδεν
αὐγὴ χαλκείη κορύθων ἄπο λαμπομενάων
θωρήκων τε νεοσμήκτων σακέων τε φαεινῶν
ἐρχομένων ἄμυδις·
sentences.tr:
osse d’ amerden
augē chalkeiē korythōn apo lampomenaōn
thōrēkōn te neosmēktōn sakeōn te phaeinōn
erchomenōn amydis·
sentences.l:
and their eyes were dazzled by
the bronze glare, from helmets gleaming
and breastplates newly polished and shields shining
coming together;
sentences.i: and the bronze glare from the gleaming helmets and the newly polished breastplates and the shining shields dazzled the eyes as they came on together;
sentences.n: The glare of the armour blinds the eye. The order is object first: ὄσσε is the dual ‘the two eyes’ (accusative), object of ἄμερδεν, an unaugmented past tense of ἀμέρδω ‘deprive, blind, dazzle’; the subject is αὐγὴ χαλκείη ‘a glare of bronze’. κορύθων ἄπο is ‘from helmets’ (ἄπο after its noun, with the accent withdrawn), and λαμπομενάων ‘gleaming’ is the epic genitive plural feminine. θωρήκων … νεοσμήκτων is ‘newly polished breastplates’ (νέος + σμήχω ‘wipe clean’), σακέων … φαεινῶν ‘shining shields’ (σάκος, epic genitive plural), and ἐρχομένων ἄμυδις ‘as they came together’, a genitive plural agreeing with those pieces of gear. The unit begins in the middle of line 340 and ends in the middle of line 343.

sentences.t:
μάλα κεν θρασυκάρδιος εἴη
ὃς τότε γηθήσειεν ἰδὼν πόνον οὐδ’ ἀκάχοιτο.
sentences.tr:
mala ken thrasykardios eiē
hos tote gēthēseien idōn ponon oud’ akachoito.
sentences.l:
Very bold-hearted would he be
who then would rejoice at seeing the toil and not be grieved.
sentences.i: Very bold-hearted would be the man who would then rejoice at the sight of the toil, and not be grieved.
sentences.n: The poet steps outside the story to say how dreadful the sight was: only a very bold-hearted man would look on it with pleasure. μάλα κεν … εἴη is ‘would be’ (κεν with the optative), θρασυκάρδιος ‘bold-hearted’ (θρασύς + καρδία), and ὃς … γηθήσειεν a relative clause with the optative, ‘who would rejoice’; ἰδών ‘on seeing’, πόνον ‘toil’, here the toil of battle, and οὐδ’ ἀκάχοιτο ‘and not be grieved’ (ἀκαχίζω). The unit begins in the middle of line 343.

sentences.t:
τὼ δ’ ἀμφὶς φρονέοντε δύω Κρόνου υἷε κραταιὼ
ἀνδράσιν ἡρώεσσιν ἐτεύχετον ἄλγεα λυγρά.
sentences.tr:
tō d’ amphis phroneonte dyō Kronou huie krataiō
andrasin hērōessin eteucheton algea lygra.
sentences.l:
And the two, thinking apart, the two sons of Cronus, strong,
for men, heroes, were contriving grievous pains.
sentences.i: But the two strong sons of Cronus, being of different minds, were contriving grievous pains for heroic men.
sentences.n: The poet turns to the gods behind the battle: the two sons of Cronus are Zeus and Poseidon, named in the next lines. τώ is the dual ‘those two’ and φρονέοντε a dual participle ‘thinking’, with ἀμφίς ‘apart, in different ways’; δύω Κρόνου υἷε κραταιώ is ‘the two sons of Cronus, strong’ (all dual; κραταιός is a by-form of κρατερός ‘strong’). ἐτεύχετον is the dual imperfect of τεύχω ‘make, contrive’. ἀνδράσιν ἡρώεσσιν is ‘for men, heroes’: ἡρώεσσιν is the epic dative plural of ἥρως, used like an adjective. ἄλγεα λυγρά are ‘grievous pains’.

sentences.t:
Ζεὺς μέν ῥα Τρώεσσι καὶ Ἕκτορι βούλετο νίκην
κυδαίνων Ἀχιλῆα πόδας ταχύν·
sentences.tr:
Zeus men rha Trōessi kai Hektori bouleto nikēn
kydainōn Achilēa podas tachyn·
sentences.l:
Zeus, indeed, for the Trojans and Hector wanted victory,
giving glory to Achilles, swift in feet;
sentences.i: Zeus wanted victory for the Trojans and Hector, giving glory to Achilles, swift of foot;
sentences.n: The two gods’ purposes: Zeus first, answered by Ποσειδάων δέ at 351. Ζεὺς μέν ῥα is ‘Zeus, then’, with Τρώεσσι καὶ Ἕκτορι (epic dative) ‘for the Trojans and Hector’ and βούλετο ‘wanted’. κυδαίνων is ‘giving glory to’ (κῦδος ‘glory’): the favour to the Trojans is the way he honours Achilles (the next unit names Thetis, his mother). Ἀχιλῆα has a single λ, and πόδας ταχύν ‘swift in feet’ is Achilles’ stock epithet (accusative of respect), translated every time. The unit ends in the middle of line 348.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τι πάμπαν
ἤθελε λαὸν ὀλέσθαι Ἀχαιϊκὸν Ἰλιόθι πρό,
ἀλλὰ Θέτιν κύδαινε καὶ υἱέα καρτερόθυμον.
sentences.tr:
oude ti pampan
ēthele laon olesthai Achaiïkon Iliothi pro,
alla Thetin kydaine kai huiea karterothymon.
sentences.l:
and not at all
wished the Achaean people to perish before Ilios,
but was giving glory to Thetis and her strong-hearted son.
sentences.i: He did not at all wish the Achaean army to perish before Ilios, but was giving glory to Thetis and her strong-hearted son.
sentences.n: Zeus’ aim is limited: honour for Achilles, not the destruction of the army. οὐδέ τι πάμπαν is ‘and not at all’ (πάμπαν reinforces the negative). ἤθελε is the imperfect of ἐθέλω ‘wish’, and ὀλέσθαι the aorist middle infinitive of ὄλλυμι ‘perish’, with λαὸν Ἀχαιϊκόν ‘the Achaean people (army)’ as its subject. Ἰλιόθι πρό is ‘before Ilios’ (the suffix -θι ‘at’, πρό after its noun). κύδαινε is the unaugmented imperfect of κυδαίνω, ‘was giving glory to’, with Θέτιν (Thetis, the mother of Achilles) and υἱέα, the epic accusative of υἱός; καρτερόθυμον ‘strong-hearted’ is a stock epithet, translated every time. The unit begins in the middle of line 348.

sentences.t:
Ἀργείους δὲ Ποσειδάων ὀρόθυνε μετελθὼν
λάθρῃ ὑπεξαναδὺς πολιῆς ἁλός·
sentences.tr:
Argeious de Poseidaōn orothyne metelthōn
lathrēi hypexanadys poliēs halos·
sentences.l:
And the Argives Poseidon roused, going among them,
in secret, having come up from under the grey sea;
sentences.i: But Poseidon went among the Argives and roused them, having come up in secret from the grey sea;
sentences.n: Poseidon, who has already been shown pitying the Achaeans (13.15–16), now acts, in opposition to Zeus. Ἀργείους is one of the three names the poet uses for the army (‘Argives’). ὀρόθυνε is the unaugmented past tense of ὀροθύνω ‘rouse’, and μετελθών the aorist participle of μετέρχομαι ‘go among’. λάθρῃ ‘in secret’; ὑπεξαναδύς is the aorist participle of ὑπεξαναδύομαι ‘come up from under’, taking the genitive πολιῆς ἁλός ‘out of the grey sea’. The unit ends in the middle of line 352.

sentences.t:
ἤχθετο γάρ ῥα
Τρωσὶν δαμναμένους, Διὶ δὲ κρατερῶς ἐνεμέσσα.
sentences.tr:
ēchtheto gar rha
Trōsin damnamenous, Dii de kraterōs enemessa.
sentences.l:
for he was distressed
that they were being subdued by the Trojans, and with Zeus strongly he felt resentment.
sentences.i: for he was distressed that they were being subdued by the Trojans, and felt strong resentment against Zeus.
sentences.n: The reason for Poseidon’s action. ἤχθετο is the imperfect of ἄχθομαι ‘be distressed’, γάρ ῥα ‘for, indeed’. Τρωσὶν δαμναμένους is an accusative plural participle, ‘(them) being subdued by the Trojans’, the unstated ‘them’ being the Argives of the last unit; Τρωσίν is the dative of the agent. Διὶ δὲ κρατερῶς ἐνεμέσσα is ‘and strongly felt resentment against Zeus’: νεμεσσάω (= νεμεσάω) takes the dative of the person, and ἐνεμέσσα is its imperfect. The second line is the same as 13.16, where Poseidon first pities the Achaeans (the first line of that pair, 13.15, has him come up out of the sea and sit down). The unit begins in the middle of line 352.

sentences.t:
ἦ μὰν ἀμφοτέροισιν ὁμὸν γένος ἠδ’ ἴα πάτρη,
ἀλλὰ Ζεὺς πρότερος γεγόνει καὶ πλείονα ᾔδη.
sentences.tr:
ē man amphoteroisin homon genos ēd’ ia patrē,
alla Zeus proteros gegonei kai pleiona ēidē.
sentences.l:
Truly to both a common race and one fatherland,
but Zeus had been born first and knew more.
sentences.i: Truly the two had a common race and one fatherland, but Zeus had been born first and knew more.
sentences.n: Why Poseidon will not oppose Zeus openly. ἦ μάν ‘truly’; ἀμφοτέροισιν ‘for both’ is a dative of possession with a verb ‘was’ understood, ‘both had’. ὁμὸν γένος is ‘a common race’, ἴα the Ionic feminine of εἷς ‘one’ (= μία), and πάτρη is ‘fatherland, ancestral stock’ (= πάτρα): the gods are brothers, both sons of Cronus (345). ἀλλά marks the difference: Ζεὺς πρότερος γεγόνει is ‘Zeus had been born first’ (the pluperfect γεγόνει), and ᾔδη the pluperfect of οἶδα ‘knew’, πλείονα ‘more things’.

sentences.t:
τώ ῥα καὶ ἀμφαδίην μὲν ἀλεξέμεναι ἀλέεινε,
λάθρῃ δ’ αἰὲν ἔγειρε κατὰ στρατὸν ἀνδρὶ ἐοικώς.
sentences.tr:
tō rha kai amphadiēn men alexemenai aleeine,
lathrēi d’ aien egeire kata straton andri eoikōs.
sentences.l:
Therefore indeed openly he shunned defending,
but in secret always he was rousing them through the army, to a man likened.
sentences.i: So he shunned defending them openly, but was always rousing them in secret through the army, like a man.
sentences.n: The consequence of Poseidon’s deference: he helps, but in disguise. τώ here is ‘therefore’ (= τῷ), not the dual. ἀμφαδίην ‘openly’ answers λάθρῃ ‘in secret’ (μέν … δέ). ἀλεξέμεναι is the epic infinitive of ἀλέξω ‘ward off, defend’, and ἀλέεινε the imperfect of ἀλεείνω ‘shun’: ‘he shunned defending (them)’. αἰέν ‘always’, ἔγειρε the unaugmented imperfect of ἐγείρω ‘rouse’ (a different verb from ὀρόθυνε ‘roused’ at 351, which the house text also renders ‘rouse’), κατὰ στρατόν ‘through the army’. ἀνδρὶ ἐοικώς is ‘like a man’ (the perfect participle of ἔοικα ‘be like’, with the dative): the god takes a man’s shape.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δ’ ἔριδος κρατερῆς καὶ ὁμοιΐου πτολέμοιο
πεῖραρ ἐπαλλάξαντες ἐπ’ ἀμφοτέροισι τάνυσσαν
ἄρρηκτόν τ’ ἄλυτόν τε, τὸ πολλῶν γούνατ’ ἔλυσεν.
sentences.tr:
toi d’ eridos kraterēs kai homoiïou ptolemoio
peirar epallaxantes ep’ amphoteroisi tanyssan
arrēkton t’ alyton te, to pollōn gounat’ elysen.
sentences.l:
And they, of strong strife and of war common to all
the cord having interlaced, over both stretched it,
unbreakable and unloosable, which the knees of many loosed.
sentences.i: And they interlaced the cord of strong strife and of the war that is common to all and stretched it over both sides, unbreakable and unloosable, a cord that has loosed the knees of many.
sentences.n: The gods’ work is pictured as a rope drawn tight over both armies. τοί is the article used as a pronoun, ‘they’, the two gods (the dual of 345 now plural). ἔριδος κρατερῆς καὶ ὁμοιΐου πτολέμοιο are genitives depending on πεῖραρ, ‘the cord of strong strife and of war common to all’; ὁμοίιος is of uncertain sense, and ‘common to all’ is the Iliad’s house rendering (the Odyssey has ‘even-handed’). πεῖραρ means ‘end, limit’ and also ‘cord, bond’; which is meant here is disputed, and ‘cord’ is chosen because it is stretched (τάνυσσαν, the unaugmented aorist of τανύω) and called ἄρρηκτον ‘unbreakable’ and ἄλυτον ‘unloosable’. ἐπαλλάξαντες is the aorist participle of ἐπαλλάσσω ‘cross over, interlace’ (the exact picture of what is done to the cord is not clear), and ἐπ’ ἀμφοτέροισι ‘over both’ sides. τὸ πολλῶν γούνατ’ ἔλυσεν is ‘which loosed the knees of many’: to loose a man’s knees is to leave him unable to stand, to kill him.
